meta.title: Vietnam's 1,500-Year Empire Lost To History: Living Relics Of Champa Kingdom | The Mark Of Empire
meta.description:
Linked to ancient seafarers from Taiwan, the Champa were expert sailors and vital players in global trade. On land, they were skilled builders and innovative agriculturalists who also made their mark on the modern world. Curator and scholar Peter Lee embarks on a quest to uncover the story of the Champa Kingdom and its glory years.

From visiting the ancient, hallowed grounds of My Son Sanctuary where grand temples showcase the king’s authority, to learning about modern Cham identity with a local rap artist, Peter traces the great heights that the kingdom reached before its eventual decline. But in recent years, a new generation of Cham people are striving for pride and recognition of their ancient heritage.

WATCH MORE The Mark of Empire: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLkMf14VQEvTbN1Gh3smAZtc2E-ACeu3Fg

00:00 Introduction
03:06 Inside Hoi An's Marble Mountains
06:26 Fishing on traditional basket boats 
09:36 Uncovering Loi Citadel excavation site
12:29 Crucial finds from Chau Tan shipwreck
16:15 Why is Agarwood so valuable?
18:54 Meeting the Jarai people
25:57 Restoring ruins of My Son Sanctuary
35:33 Exploring the Duong Long towers
40:02 Passing down Cham script
42:26 Modern ways of preserving Cham history

==============================
ABOUT The Mark of Empire: Kingdoms of the Sea:
What are the secrets and mysteries behind Asia’s ancient empires? In the third season of this award-winning series, curator and scholar Peter Lee is back on a journey to trace clues and uncover new theories behind the Srivijaya empire, the Champa kingdom, the Sultanate of Sulu, and the Anuradhapura kingdom. What were the epic battles, political alliances and cultural exchanges forged by the four powers in the region?

From investigating the iconic reliefs of Borobudur temple in Indonesia, to diving for sea cucumbers in the Philippines’ Sulu Archipelago, to practicing the ancient martial art of Angampora in Sri Lanka, and learning about modern Cham rap music in Vietnam, Peter traces the rise and fall of these formidable kingdoms, and the cultural legacies that they have left on the region until today.

comments.author: @nguyentandat2001
comments.text:
As a Vietnamese person (ethnically Kinh), I want to speak frankly but respectfully to some foreign friends, especially Cham Muslims in Cambodia and parts of the Muslim community in Malaysia that claiming Cham heritage in Vietnam as “yours” lacks any serious academic basis. For most of its history, Champa was an Indianized kingdom, deeply shaped by Hinduism (Shaivism and Vaishnavism) and later Buddhism, with the Cham language belonging to the Austronesian family and a cultural identity distinct from the Malay–Islamic world.

In present-day Vietnam, the Cham community is officially recognized as having three main groups: Cham Bàlamôn (Ahiêr) and Cham Bàni (Awal), two long-established indigenous communities concentrated in Ninh Thuận and Bình Thuận, which are historically the heartland of Champa; and Cham Islam (orthodox Sunni), a later formation resulting from trade networks and Islamic missionary activities, mainly found in An Giang and parts of southern Vietnam. To attribute the entirety of Champa’s temples, art, religious practices, and customary laws to Islam or to “Malay culture” is a misrepresentation of history. Islam in the Cham context is a later layer of cultural adaptation, not the civilizational foundation of Champa. Mutual respect must begin with respect for historical facts: Champa’s heritage belongs to the Cham people, is preserved in Vietnam, and cannot be appropriated through oversimplified narratives or contemporary identity politics.

You can still find descendants of the Cham people living around Hanoi today. When Dai Viet defeated Champa centuries ago, they brought Cham court ladies and skilled craftsmen back to the northern capital. Over time, their descendants settled in different villages in the area.
In my village, we grow a lot of coconut trees. People say the coconut seeds were first brought here long ago by Cham captives. Even the way we speak sounds quite different from the standard Northern Vietnamese accent. Some believe it may be the result of generations of blending between Cham and Kinh tones.

comments.text:
I was quite interested in Vietnam history  before I travel to Vietnam recently. 
It may surprise many, but I believe the Campa people could have Indian or even Sri Lankan origins. In Sri Lanka, the worship of Lord Shiva dates back to very ancient times. Long ago, the Naga clan — one of the earliest known Sri Lankan communities — lived as skilled sea traders, connecting with many cultures around the world. Their symbol was the snake, which they proudly used as their emblem.

They were wealthy merchants who traded spices, pearls, gems, and metals. In ancient times, weaving was an important craft used to make clothing — something we also see in Cham culture. Even today, betel leaves and areca nut are used in auspicious events and when inviting priests, a tradition shared across many South and Southeast Asian cultures.

It is possible that one group of these prosperous sea merchants settled in a new land and eventually established their own kingdom. Later, with Chinese influence, their language, physical features, and cultural expressions may have evolved. However, ancestor worship is still practiced among many tribal communities, preserving a connection to the past.

No one can firmly claim a single origin, because the people of these regions are deeply mixed — influenced by Indian, Chinese, Arab, and later Western colonization. Original traditions naturally changed, and new traditions developed through these interactions. The same has happened to us in Sri Lanka. Some still argue about “pure origins,” without realizing that our own heritage has also been shaped by centuries of cultural exchange.

With globalization, cultures continue to change rapidly. The younger generation around the world often looks and lives similarly. Change is the ultimate reality. 😊❤
